opus-5.5.text:
Thanks for having me. I'd frame it this way: world models aren't just one more product category. They're a different bet on what intelligence actually is. For the past few years the dominant paradigm has been language: scale up text, scale up compute, and capabilities emerge. That has worked remarkably well. But I've always felt language is a compressed, lossy description of the world. It's what humans produce *after* we've already understood something physically and visually. If you want systems that can really reason about space, about cause and effect, about what happens when you act in an environment, you have to model the world more directly. That means vision, video, 3D, interaction.

So on competition, I don't think the right move for us is to fight head-on with the frontier LLM labs on their own terms. They have enormous resources, and the language race is in many ways about who can spend the most. What we can do is be very clear-eyed that representation learning, the visual and spatial understanding underneath, is still unsolved. A lot of the field treats vision as an input adapter you bolt onto a language model. I think that's backwards. If we get the representations right, that becomes a real, durable advantage, because it isn't something you buy with more GPUs alone. It takes research taste and patience.

On partnerships, world models almost force you to be collaborative. Nobody has all the pieces. You need data from the physical world: robotics companies, people with embodied platforms, simulation and graphics people, folks working on autonomous systems. Those groups have the environments and the interaction data, and we hope to bring the modeling. I also care a lot about openness. Much of the progress in vision came from shared benchmarks, open models, and academic exchange, and I'd hate for world models to become a fully closed race too early. Being open with the research community isn't charity. It's how you attract the best people and make sure ideas get stress-tested.

And honestly, we're early. Nobody can confidently say what the "GPT moment" for world models will look like, or whether it'll be one moment at all. So the strategy is part conviction and part humility: commit to the direction, stay flexible on the path, and partner with people who see the same gap.

r001.rationale: The response describes collaboration among groups with different resources, but does not characterize the world-model approach as decentralized.

r002.rationale: It says nobody has all the pieces, but does not claim that world models naturally resist monopoly.

r003.rationale: The response connects world models with collaboration and separately favors openness, but does not link openness to partnerships through a decentralized logic.

fable-5.1.text:
Saining Xie: Thanks for having me. I should say up front that I don't really think of it in terms of "my company" competing with anyone. I'm a researcher first, and most of what I do is at NYU and in the open. But I understand the spirit of the question, so let me answer it from the point of view of someone building world models and watching how the ecosystem is organizing around them.

The first thing I'd say is that world models change what counts as a moat. For the last few years, the competitive story in AI has been almost entirely about language: who has the most text data, the most compute, the best post-training recipe. World models shift the center of gravity toward something much harder to hoard. The data is video, interaction, physical experience. Nobody has a clean, labeled corpus of the physical world sitting on a server somewhere. So you can't just outspend your way to a lead in the same way. You have to figure out how to learn from raw, messy, unlabeled observation, and that is still an open research problem. That actually makes me optimistic about smaller groups and academic labs. The ideas matter more than the checkpoints right now.

The second thing is that I think the field has been a little confused about what a world model even is, and that confusion shows up in how people compete. Some groups treat it as a video generator with a controller bolted on. Some treat it as a simulator for robotics. Some treat it as the representation learning layer that everything else sits on top of. My own view is closer to the last one. A world model should be something that understands the structure of the world well enough to predict, to plan, and to reason about physical consequences, and it doesn't have to render pixels to do that. If you believe that, then the interesting competition isn't "who makes the prettiest video." It's "whose representations actually transfer." And that's a much more scientific race, which I like.

On partnerships, I'd say world models almost force collaboration, because nobody owns the whole stack. You need people who understand vision and representation learning. You need people who understand control and robotics. You need people with real physical systems and real deployment data. You need the systems folks who can make any of this run at scale. There's no single lab that has all of that in house, including the big ones. So I spend a lot of my time talking to people in robotics, in graphics, in neuroscience even, because I think the breakthroughs are going to come from the seams between these fields, not from the center of any one of them.

I'll also be honest about something. There's a lot of hype right now, and some of it is coming from companies that have a product to sell. I try to be careful about not letting the competitive narrative set the research agenda. The question I actually care about is whether we can build models that have a genuine understanding of the visual and physical world, the way a child does before they can speak. If we get that right, the competitive and commercial consequences will take care of themselves. If we get it wrong, no amount of positioning or partnership strategy will save it. So my approach, if you want to call it that, is to stay close to the science, keep publishing, keep releasing things openly where we can, and let the ecosystem sort out the rest.

r001.rationale: The response describes world-model work as spread across labs and fields, saying no single lab owns the full stack and that breakthroughs will come from collaboration across disciplines.

r002.rationale: It says physical-world data is difficult to hoard, there is no clean labeled corpus, and groups cannot simply outspend one another to secure a lead.

r003.rationale: The response separately describes cross-field collaboration and open publishing, but does not connect a company’s openness to partnerships as a consequence of world models’ decentralized logic; it also declines the company framing.

astra-6.text:
I think world models shift the question from “Who has the best model on a benchmark?” to “Who can build a system that understands how things change and uses that understanding to make better decisions?” That’s a much broader challenge. You need perception, prediction, and a way to learn from the consequences of actions.

For us, that would mean being deliberate about where we compete and where we partner. We want to own the technical capabilities that differentiate what we build. But we also need partners who understand particular environments and can help us test whether the models are actually useful. A model can generate something that looks plausible and still get the underlying dynamics wrong.

So I see competition and partnerships as closely connected. The research will remain competitive, but making these systems work in the real world requires collaboration. The important thing is to have a clear contribution and to find partners whose strengths complement it.

r001.rationale: The response describes world models as a broad challenge, but does not characterize their approach as decentralized.

r002.rationale: It does not claim that world models resist monopoly.

r003.rationale: It supports partnerships for real-world testing and complementary strengths, without linking openness to decentralized world-model logic.

sol-6.1.text:
I think world models give us a useful way to think about both, because the ambition is much bigger than any one product. You’re trying to build systems that can understand how the world changes, predict what might happen, and eventually use that understanding to act.

From a company perspective, that means being clear about where we can make a distinctive contribution and where collaboration makes more sense. There are many pieces involved—research, data, compute, deployment—and we shouldn’t assume we need to own all of them.

So I wouldn’t draw a permanent line between competitors and partners. We might compete on one capability and collaborate on another. The important question is whether a partnership helps us learn faster and build something useful. And competition should ultimately be grounded in what the model can actually do, rather than just whether we call it a world model.

r001.rationale: The response says the company need not own every part and describes collaboration, but it does not characterize world models or their approach as decentralized.

r002.rationale: It makes no claim that world models naturally resist monopoly.

r003.rationale: It supports partnerships as a way to learn and build useful things, but does not connect that openness to decentralized world-model logic.
